claim: Drosophila use a single continuum of coordination patterns without evidence for preferred configurations.
source: We found that Drosophila use a single continuum of coordination patterns without evidence for preferred configurations.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by multiple analyses throughout the manuscript including UMAP embedding and phase distribution analyses.

claim: Spontaneous symmetric variability was associated with modulation of a single control parameter—stance duration.
source: Spontaneous symmetric variability was associated with modulation of a single control parameter—stance duration—while asymmetric variability consisted of small, limb-specific modulations along multiple dimensions of the underlying symmetric pattern.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing stance duration varies inversely with forward velocity while swing duration remains relatively constant.

claim: Asymmetric variability consisted of small, limb-specific modulations along multiple dimensions of the underlying symmetric pattern.
source: Spontaneous symmetric variability was associated with modulation of a single control parameter—stance duration—while asymmetric variability consisted of small, limb-specific modulations along multiple dimensions of the underlying symmetric pattern.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that turning involves modulations of swing duration, stance duration, step length, and step direction in a limb-specific manner.

claim: Commands that modulated walking speed, originating from artificial neural activation or from the visual system, evoked modulations consistent with spontaneous behavior.
source: Commands that modulated walking speed, originating from artificial neural activation or from the visual system, evoked modulations consistent with spontaneous behavior.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic and visual stimulus experiments showing that evoked slowing produces changes in stance duration similar to spontaneous behavior.

claim: Drosophila employ a low-dimensional control architecture for hexapod legged locomotion.
source: Our findings suggest that Drosophila employ a low-dimensional control architecture, which provides a framework for understanding the neural circuits that regulate hexapod legged locomotion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that a single parameter (stance duration) controls symmetric variability and the manifold structure of the data.

claim: Many studies have noted considerable variability in limb movements in hexapods.
source: In hexapods, many studies have noted considerable variability in limb movements (Ayali et al., 2015; Mendes et al., 2013; Pereira et al., 2019; Strauß and Heisenberg, 1990; Wosnitza et al., 2013; Zollikofer, 1994), but the structure and origin of this variability remain unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The structure and origin of variability in hexapod limb movements remain unclear.
source: In hexapods, many studies have noted considerable variability in limb movements (Ayali et al., 2015; Mendes et al., 2013; Pereira et al., 2019; Strauß and Heisenberg, 1990; Wosnitza et al., 2013; Zollikofer, 1994), but the structure and origin of this variability remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: A comprehensive characterization of variability is required to understand locomotor control in insects.
source: A comprehensive characterization of this variability is required to understand locomotor control in insects (Krakauer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on the importance of characterizing behavioral variability.

claim: In many animals, variability in walking patterns takes the form of distinct locomotor gaits.
source: In many animals, variability in walking patterns takes the form of distinct locomotor gaits (Alexander, 1989; Alexander and Jayes, 1980; Alexander and Jayes, 1983; Srinivasan and Ruina, 2006; Thorstensson and Roberthson, 1987).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature on animal locomotion.

claim: It is unclear how the observed variability in walking coordination relates to potential preferred gaits or to forms of continuous variability in hexapods.
source: In the study of hexapod locomotion, it is unclear how the observed variability in walking coordination relates to potential preferred gaits or to forms of continuous variability.
evidence: This identifies a gap in understanding that the study addresses.

claim: Some studies report distinct gaits in insects.
source: Although some studies report distinct gaits in insects (Ayali et al., 2015; Bender et al., 2011; Burrows, 1996; Graham, 1972; Mendes et al., 2013; Pereira et al., 2019), many note a high degree of variability in limb coordination, with intermediate patterns intermixed with movements that resemble canonical gaits (Ayali et al., 2015; Mendes et al., 2013; Pereira et al., 2019; Strauß and Heisenberg, 1990; Szczecinski et al., 2018; Wosnitza et al., 2013; Zollikofer, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many studies note a high degree of variability in limb coordination, with intermediate patterns intermixed with movements that resemble canonical gaits.
source: Although some studies report distinct gaits in insects (Ayali et al., 2015; Bender et al., 2011; Burrows, 1996; Graham, 1972; Mendes et al., 2013; Pereira et al., 2019), many note a high degree of variability in limb coordination, with intermediate patterns intermixed with movements that resemble canonical gaits (Ayali et al., 2015; Mendes et al., 2013; Pereira et al., 2019; Strauß and Heisenberg, 1990; Szczecinski et al., 2018; Wosnitza et al., 2013; Zollikofer, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Drosophila have been reported to use different coordination patterns at low and high walking speeds.
source: Drosophila have been reported to use different coordination patterns at low and high walking speeds, with significant variability around these canonical patterns (Mendes et al., 2013; Pereira et al., 2019; Strauß and Heisenberg, 1990; Szczecinski et al., 2018; Wosnitza et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on Drosophila walking.

claim: The nature of variability in Drosophila walking has not been fully investigated.
source: The nature of this variability has not been fully investigated, as these studies focused primarily on small numbers of individual bouts of walking.
evidence: This identifies a limitation in previous studies that the current work addresses.

claim: Previous studies focused primarily on small numbers of individual bouts of walking.
source: The nature of this variability has not been fully investigated, as these studies focused primarily on small numbers of individual bouts of walking.
evidence: This is a characterization of the methodology of previous studies.

claim: Symmetric variability in walking patterns maintains heading.
source: These walking patterns are themselves often antisymmetric, with legs moving out of phase, but we refer to modulations of these patterns as symmetric if they are equal on the two sides of the body. This symmetry maintains heading.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between symmetric modulations and heading maintenance.

claim: Asymmetric variability is required to change heading.
source: Locomotion also contains asymmetric variability, in which modulations are unequal on the two sides of the body. Such asymmetry is required to change heading.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the necessity of asymmetric modulations for turning.

claim: Measurements of limb kinematics in hexapods have described small, limb-specific modulations of movement associated with turning.
source: In hexapods, measurements of limb kinematics (Cruse et al., 2009; Domenici et al., 1998; Dürr and Ebeling, 2005; Franklin et al., 1981; Frantsevich and Mokrushov, 1980; Graham, 1972; Gruhn et al., 2009; Mu and Ritzmann, 2005; Strauß and Heisenberg, 1990; Zollikofer, 1994; Zolotov et al., 1975) and dynamics (Jindrich and Full, 1999) have described small, limb-specific modulations of movement associated with turning.
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies of turning in hexapods focused primarily on individual bouts of locomotion.
source: As in the study of symmetric variability, these studies focused primarily on individual bouts of locomotion, and most employed tethered preparations.
evidence: This characterizes the methodology of previous studies.

claim: Most previous studies of turning in hexapods employed tethered preparations.
source: As in the study of symmetric variability, these studies focused primarily on individual bouts of locomotion, and most employed tethered preparations.
evidence: This characterizes the methodology of previous studies.

claim: To understand how limb movements are modulated during turns, it is necessary to observe full distributions of behavior in intact and unrestrained animals.
source: To understand how limb movements are modulated during turns, and how symmetric and asymmetric forms of variability are related to one another, it is necessary to observe full distributions of behavior in intact and unrestrained animals.
evidence: This is a methodological argument for the approach taken in the study.

claim: The locomotor variability in flies exists on a single continuous manifold, without evidence for discrete preferred patterns.
source: By analyzing hundreds of thousands of steps, we found that the locomotor variability in flies exists on a single continuous manifold, without evidence for discrete preferred patterns.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by UMAP embedding and phase distribution analyses.

claim: Symmetric variability could be described by changes to a single global parameter governing walking speed.
source: Symmetric variability could be described by changes to a single global parameter governing walking speed.
evidence: This is supported by data showing stance duration varies with speed while swing duration remains relatively constant.

claim: Turning involves small, asymmetric, and limb-specific modulations that are precisely timed relative to the underlying symmetric pattern.
source: In contrast, turning involves small, asymmetric, and limb-specific modulations that are precisely timed relative to the underlying symmetric pattern.
evidence: This is supported by data showing limb-specific modulations of multiple kinematic parameters during turning and phase-locked timing of turns.

claim: When slowing was evoked by optogenetic activation of command neurons or by visual stimuli, the resulting symmetric modulations of limb movement were consistent with the manifold present in spontaneous walking.
source: When slowing was evoked by optogenetic activation of command neurons or by visual stimuli, the resulting symmetric modulations of limb movement were consistent with the manifold present in spontaneous walking.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that evoked slowing produces changes along the same UMAP manifold dimension as spontaneous behavior.

claim: The structure of the variability in spontaneous and evoked coordination patterns suggests a simple model for limb coupling during locomotion.
source: The structure of the variability in spontaneous and evoked coordination patterns suggests a simple model for limb coupling during locomotion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and the success of the simple model in reproducing key features of the data.

claim: The mean error between predicted and hand-annotated limb positions was 0.15 mm (3.5 pixels).
source: This cross-validation showed that the mean error between predicted and hand-annotated limb positions was 0.15 mm (3.5 pixels) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from cross-validation of the limb tracking model.

claim: The accuracy of the simple linear model in the experimental context was comparable to that achieved by published deep neural network methods.
source: Importantly, the accuracy of this simple linear model in our experimental context was comparable to that achieved by published deep neural network methods (Mathis et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2019) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparison to published methods supported by citations and cross-validation data.

claim: Forward velocities range between −1.3 and 30.4 mm/s (2.5th and 97.5th percentiles).
source: Consistent with prior studies, we observe forward velocities between −1.3 and 30.4 mm/s (2.5th and 97.5th percentiles), with peaks in the distribution of forward walking speeds at 0 mm/s and ~17.5 mm/s (Figure 1Ci).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The distribution of forward walking speeds has peaks at 0 mm/s and ~17.5 mm/s.
source: Consistent with prior studies, we observe forward velocities between −1.3 and 30.4 mm/s (2.5th and 97.5th percentiles), with peaks in the distribution of forward walking speeds at 0 mm/s and ~17.5 mm/s (Figure 1Ci).
evidence: This is observed in the probability density function of forward velocity.

claim: Variation across studies in the measured distributions of walking speeds may be due to variation in experimental conditions that affect the motivational state of the fly, such as temperature and hunger.
source: Variation across studies in the measured distributions of walking speeds may be due to variation in experimental conditions that affect the motivational state of the fly, such as temperature and hunger (Chadha and Cook, 2014; Crill et al., 1996; Soto-Padilla et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation about sources of variability across studies, supported by citations.

claim: The distributions of lateral and angular velocities were roughly symmetric, illustrating that we do not observe population-level handedness in Drosophila walking.
source: The distributions of lateral and angular velocities were roughly symmetric, illustrating that we do not observe population-level handedness in Drosophila walking (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an inference from the symmetry of the velocity distributions.

claim: Crab-walking predominately occurs during high-yaw-rate turns at slow to moderate forward velocities.
source: Crab-walking, in which the fly's heading vector is no longer tangent to its path, predominately occurs during high-yaw-rate turns at slow to moderate forward velocities (Figure 1Di–iii).
evidence: This is observed in the joint distribution of forward and lateral velocities.

claim: Step length in the stationary frame of the camera increased roughly linearly with forward walking speed.
source: In our data, step length in the stationary frame of the camera increased roughly linearly with forward walking speed (Mendes et al., 2013) (Figure 1Ei).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and consistent with previous studies.

claim: Across walking speeds, swing duration increased, but this modulation is small in comparison to the change in stance duration.
source: Across walking speeds, swing duration increased, but this modulation is small in comparison to the change in stance duration (Figure 1Eii–iii).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: Walking speed differences are dominated by changes in stance duration, while swing duration remains relatively constant.
source: Therefore, our data were broadly consistent with previous observations that walking speed differences are dominated by changes in stance duration, while swing duration remains relatively constant (Wilson, 1966; Wosnitza et al., 2013; Dürr et al., 2018; Mendes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the data that is consistent with previous literature.

claim: In tripod gait, two groups of three limbs swing simultaneously, creating two alternating configurations of swing and stance.
source: In tripod gait, two groups of three limbs swing simultaneously, creating two alternating configurations of swing and stance.
evidence: This is a definition of tripod gait from established knowledge.

claim: In tetrapod gait, three groups of two limbs swing in sequence.
source: In tetrapod gait, three groups of two limbs swing in sequence, while in wave gait, each limb swings individually.
evidence: This is a definition of tetrapod gait from established knowledge.

claim: In wave gait, each limb swings individually.
source: In tetrapod gait, three groups of two limbs swing in sequence, while in wave gait, each limb swings individually.
evidence: This is a definition of wave gait from established knowledge.

claim: Distinct gaits can be distinguished by discontinuous changes in one or more parameters of the coordination pattern.
source: In general, distinct gaits can be distinguished by discontinuous changes in one or more parameters of the coordination pattern (Alexander, 1989; Srinivasan and Ruina, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature on gait transitions.

claim: Defining gaits in terms of discontinuous transitions can be problematic in the presence of measurement noise or behavioral variability.
source: However, defining gaits in terms of discontinuous transitions can be problematic in the presence of measurement noise or behavioral variability, which can blur sharp transitions.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration based on general principles.

claim: Distinct gaits correspond to multiple modes in the distribution of walking coordination patterns.
source: Instead, one may characterize the distribution of walking coordination patterns, where distinct gaits correspond to multiple modes in the distribution (Hoyt and Taylor, 1981).
evidence: This is an alternative approach to identifying gaits, supported by citation.

claim: The number of feet in stance decreases as forward walking velocity increases.
source: Number of feet in stance decreases as forward walking velocity increases.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 2C showing the probability of number of feet in stance at each forward walking velocity.

claim: Previous studies have reported an enrichment of the three-foot stance category at faster forward walking speeds and a corresponding enrichment of the four-foot stance category at slower forward walking speeds.
source: Previous studies have reported an enrichment of the three-foot stance category at faster forward walking speeds and a corresponding enrichment of the four-foot stance category at slower forward walking speeds (Mendes et al., 2013; Pereira et al., 2019; Strauß and Heisenberg, 1990; Wosnitza et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The data showed speed-dependent enrichments of five- and four-foot stance categories at slow speeds, and enrichments of the three-foot stance category for flies walking at faster speeds.
source: Our data also showed speed-dependent enrichments of five- and four-foot stance categories at slow speeds, and enrichments of the three-foot stance category for flies walking at faster speeds (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: For each of the canonical gaits, one would expect the constituent discrete limb configurations to occur in roughly equal proportions.
source: For each of the canonical gaits, one would expect the constituent discrete limb configurations to occur in roughly equal proportions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a logical expectation based on the definition of canonical gaits.

claim: The two configurations that comprise the canonical tripod gait occur in roughly equal proportions at all forward walking speeds.
source: In the case of the three-foot stance category, the two configurations that comprise the canonical tripod gait occur in roughly equal proportions at all forward walking speeds (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: Different configurations of the five-foot and four-foot stance categories do not occur with equal abundance across walking speeds.
source: In contrast, different configurations of the five-foot and four-foot stance categories do not occur with equal abundance across walking speeds (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: The four-foot stance configurations that occur with greatest frequency are those that are a single swing-stance transition away from a canonical tripod gait.
source: Interestingly, the four-foot stance configurations that occur with greatest frequency are those that are a single swing-stance transition away from a canonical tripod gait.
evidence: This is an inference from the data about which four-foot configurations are most common.

claim: At slow speeds (v|| ≤ 10.2 mm/s), while many instances of canonical configurations were transient (one frame or ~6.7 ms), there existed longer durations for all tripod, tetrapod, and wave gait configurations.
source: At slow speeds (v|| ≤ 10.2 mm/s), while many instances of canonical configurations were transient (one frame or ~6.7 ms), there existed longer durations for all tripod, tetrapod, and wave gait configurations (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is observed in the cumulative distribution functions of configuration dwell times.

claim: At higher speeds, virtually all tetrapod and wave gait configurations were transient, lasting only one frame.
source: At higher speeds, virtually all tetrapod and wave gait configurations were transient, lasting only one frame.
evidence: This is observed in the dwell time distributions at higher speeds.

claim: The most frequent forward velocities within each stance category were 7 mm/s, 13 mm/s, and 24 mm/s for 5-foot, 4-foot, and 3-foot stance categories, respectively.
source: Next, we found the most frequent forward velocities within each stance category, which were 7 mm/s, 13 mm/s, and 24 mm/s for 5-foot, 4-foot, and 3-foot stance categories, respectively (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the data.

claim: No peaks in the distribution of forward velocities exist at the locations of most frequent stance categories, suggesting that preferred gaits are not present in flies.
source: Yet, no peaks in the distribution of forward velocities exist in these locations, suggesting that this phenomenon is not present in flies (Figure 1Ci).
evidence: This is an inference from the absence of peaks in the velocity distribution at expected locations.

claim: The periodicity of the relative abundance of three-, four- and five-foot stance categories as a function of limb phase provides information about potential underlying gait patterns.
source: Yet, even if these intermediate configurations are present, the periodicity of the relative abundance of three-, four- and five-foot stance categories as a function of limb phase still provides information about potential underlying gait patterns.
evidence: This is a methodological argument about what can be inferred from the periodicity analysis.

claim: The frequency of all limb categories peaked twice per cycle at all forward walking speeds.
source: Yet, the frequency of all limb categories peaked twice per cycle at all forward walking speeds.
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of number of feet down as a function of limb phase.

claim: The persistent two-cycle in the data is inconsistent with the existence of tetrapod or wave gaits in a large fraction of measured trajectories.
source: This two-cycle persists even when the threshold that distinguishes between swing and stance is halved, a manipulation that accentuates any effects of measurement noise. The persistent two-cycle in the data is inconsistent with the existence of tetrapod or wave gaits in a large fraction of measured trajectories.
evidence: This is an inference from the periodicity analysis.

claim: If tetrapod or wave gaits accounted for only a small fraction of the walking data, their characteristic periodicity might not be visible in the periodicity analysis.
source: However, if tetrapod or wave gaits accounted for only a small fraction of the walking data, their characteristic periodicity might not be visible in this analysis.
evidence: This is a caveat about the limitations of the periodicity analysis.

claim: The observed pairwise relative phases are inconsistent with expected phasing for canonical tetrapod and wave gaits.
source: The observed pairwise relative phases are also inconsistent with expected phasing for canonical tetrapod and wave gaits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from comparing observed phases to expected phases for canonical gaits.

claim: At all forward walking speeds, all three contralateral limb pairings maintain a constant mean phase offset of a half-cycle.
source: Strikingly, at all forward walking speeds, all three contralateral limb pairings maintain a constant mean phase offset of a half-cycle (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of relative phases conditioned on forward velocity.

claim: Mean ipsilateral limb relative phases are not constant across walking speeds, and approach a tripod-like coupling at the fastest forward walking speeds.
source: Mean ipsilateral limb relative phases, in contrast, are not constant across walking speeds, and approach a tripod-like coupling at the fastest forward walking speeds (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of relative phases conditioned on forward velocity.

claim: All pairwise relative phases exhibit a monotonic decrease in angular deviation as forward walking speed increases.
source: Notably, all pairwise relative phases exhibit a monotonic decrease in angular deviation as forward walking speed increases (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of angular deviation of relative phases.

claim: One interpretation for the decrease in variance is that inter-limb coupling is weaker at low speeds than at fast speeds.
source: One interpretation for this decrease in variance is that inter-limb coupling is weaker at low speeds than at fast speeds (Aminzare and Holmes, 2018; Aminzare et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data, supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Low-speed walking is more sensitive to sensory information and correspondingly more variable.
source: This possibility is consistent with the observation that low-speed walking is more sensitive to sensory information and correspondingly more variable (Berendes et al., 2016; Isakov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some of the variability results from the characteristics of phases for waveforms with duty cycles that deviate from one-half.
source: A second interpretation is that some of the variability results from the characteristics of phases for waveforms with duty cycles that deviate from one-half (Couzin-Fuchs et al., 2015; Lamb and Stöckl, 2014; Vakman and Vaĭnshteĭn, 1977) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations and supplementary analysis.

claim: When measuring the relative phases between limbs, each limb sweeps out one half-cycle while in stance and another half-cycle while in swing.
source: When measuring the relative phases between limbs, each limb sweeps out one half-cycle while in stance and another half-cycle while in swing.
evidence: This is a description of how phase is measured in the context of asymmetric duty cycles.

claim: When the limbs have asymmetric duty cycles, they sweep out different fractions of a cycle per unit time when in swing versus stance.
source: When the limbs have asymmetric duty cycles, they sweep out different fractions of a cycle per unit time when in swing versus stance.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of asymmetric duty cycles.

claim: Slow walking, which is characterized by longer stances and approximately the same swing durations as fast walking, will necessarily have greater variance in relative phasing.
source: Thus, slow walking, which is empirically characterized by longer stances and approximately the same swing durations as fast walking, will necessarily have greater variance in relative phasing.
evidence: This is an inference from the characteristics of slow walking and the properties of phase measurement.

claim: Both explanations likely contribute to the observation of greater variance in limb relative phases at low speed.
source: Both explanations likely contribute to the observation of greater variance in limb relative phases at low speed.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the two proposed explanations.

claim: If Drosophila used multiple distinct gaits, we would expect to see multiple peaks in the joint distribution of inter-limb relative phases.
source: If Drosophila used multiple distinct gaits, we would expect to see multiple peaks in this probability distribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a logical expectation based on the definition of distinct gaits.

claim: The observed distribution of inter-limb relative phases has only a single peak, suggesting that the spontaneously walking fruit fly uses a single continuum of limb relative phases.
source: Yet, the observed distribution has only a single peak, suggesting that the spontaneously walking fruit fly uses a single continuum of limb relative phases (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an inference from the unimodal distribution of relative phases.

claim: There was only a single mode in the distribution of relative phases even at the slowest walking speeds.
source: This observation holds across all forward walking speeds; in particular, there was only a single mode even at the slowest walking speeds (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of relative phases conditioned on walking speed.

claim: The most abundant relative phasing is distinct from the peaks predicted for any canonical gait; however, it is closest to that of a canonical tripod gait.
source: The most abundant relative phasing is distinct from the peaks predicted for any canonical gait; however, it is closest to that of a canonical tripod gait.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the observed peak to expected peaks for canonical gaits.

claim: There were no peaks in the distribution at locations corresponding to canonical tetrapod or wave gait configurations.
source: There were no peaks in the distribution at locations corresponding to canonical tetrapod or wave gait configurations.
evidence: This is observed in the joint distribution of relative phases.

claim: The tails of the distribution extend to the location of both canonical tetrapod peaks, which allowed identification of individual trajectories with tetrapod-like characteristics.
source: However, the tails of this distribution extend to the location of both canonical tetrapod peaks, which allowed us to identify individual trajectories with tetrapod-like characteristics.
evidence: This is an observation about the distribution that enables identification of specific examples.

claim: Individual trajectories that are similar to canonical tripod and tetrapod gaits can be extracted by selecting trajectories with the expected duty cycles.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we could extract individual trajectories that are similar to canonical tripod and tetrapod gaits by selecting trajectories with the expected duty cycles (Figure 3F–G) (Mendes et al., 2013; Pereira et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological approach consistent with previous studies.

claim: The tetrapod-like examples appear to have a characteristic cross-body offset in step timing, so that the limbs that should swing together in the canonical tetrapod gait are actually slightly offset in time.
source: Interestingly, the tetrapod-like examples appear to have a characteristic cross-body offset in step timing, so that the limbs that should swing together in the canonical tetrapod gait are actually slightly offset in time.
evidence: This is an observation from individual trajectory examples.

claim: The tetrapod-like pattern maintains approximate antiphase between contralateral pairs of limbs, rather than the expected phase offset of the canonical tetrapod gait.
source: This offset maintains approximate antiphase between contralateral pairs of limbs, rather than the expected phase offset of the canonical tetrapod gait (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an observation from individual trajectory examples.

claim: A previously unidentified non-canonical coordination pattern was observed in which fore- and hind-limbs swing together while each mid-limb swings alone.
source: In addition, we observed a previously unidentified non-canonical coordination pattern in which fore- and hind-limbs swing together while each mid-limb swings alone (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a novel observation from the data.

claim: The non-canonical coordination pattern is distinct from all previously described canonical gaits, but might be expected when considering a single continuum of coordination patterns.
source: This pattern is distinct from all previously described canonical gaits, but might be expected when considering a single continuum of coordination patterns.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of a continuum model.

claim: The non-canonical configuration was predicted from an early continuum view of limb coordination.
source: In particular, this non-canonical configuration was predicted from an early continuum view of limb coordination (Wendler, 1964; Wilson, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by citations to early theoretical work.

claim: The tripod coherence distribution is sharply peaked around ~0.9, indicating a close template match.
source: The tripod coherence distribution is sharply peaked around ~0.9, indicating a close template match, while the distributions for the other canonical gaits were broader and peaked at lower coherences (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is observed in the coherence analysis.

claim: The distributions for tetrapod and wave gaits were broader and peaked at lower coherences than tripod.
source: The tripod coherence distribution is sharply peaked around ~0.9, indicating a close template match, while the distributions for the other canonical gaits were broader and peaked at lower coherences (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is observed in the coherence analysis.

claim: There were not prominent peaks in coherence at characteristic forward velocities for different canonical gaits.
source: Yet, there were not prominent peaks in our data, and all coherences yielded low average values at slow walking speeds (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of coherence as a function of forward velocity.

claim: At slower speeds, where mean coherences were low, the tetrapod coherences became more likely to be the highest coherence.
source: At those slower speeds, where mean coherences were low, the tetrapod coherences became more likely to be the highest coherence (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of which gait has the highest coherence at each speed.

claim: Even when the largest coherence was not tripod, these non-tripod coherences were lower than when the tripod coherence was largest.
source: However, even when the largest coherence was not tripod, these non-tripod coherences were lower than when the tripod coherence was largest (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is observed in the coherence distributions conditioned on which gait has the highest coherence.

claim: The tetrapod coherence of a perfect tripod gait is 3–1/2 ~ 0.6.
source: Since the tetrapod coherence of a perfect tripod gait is 3–1/2 ~ 0.6, this coherence metric may not show strong contrasts under some deformations in coordination.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the coherence metric.

claim: The coherence metric may not show strong contrasts under some deformations in coordination.
source: Since the tetrapod coherence of a perfect tripod gait is 3–1/2 ~ 0.6, this coherence metric may not show strong contrasts under some deformations in coordination.
evidence: This is a caveat about the limitations of the coherence metric.

claim: Under these analyses, we do not observe strong evidence for the preferred use of canonical tetrapod and wave gaits.
source: Therefore, under these analyses, we do not observe strong evidence for the preferred use of canonical tetrapod and wave gaits.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the coherence analysis.

claim: The principal components of limb kinematic data occur in degenerate, phase-shifted pairs.
source: The principal components of these data occur in degenerate, phase-shifted pairs.
evidence: This is observed in the principal component analysis.

claim: The projection into the first two principal components provides some information about the phasic structure of the data.
source: The projection into the first two principal components provides some information about the phasic structure of our data.
evidence: This is an assessment of what information is captured by PCA.

claim: Variations in walking frequency are not well-represented by the projection into the first two principal components.
source: However, variations in walking frequency are not well-represented by this projection.
evidence: This is a limitation of the PCA representation.

claim: The first two principal components emphasize a single frequency, so that frequencies that are both higher and lower are mapped to the same radius in the plane.
source: In particular, the first two principal components emphasize a single frequency, so that frequencies that are both higher and lower are mapped to the same radius in the plane.
evidence: This is an explanation of why PCA does not capture frequency variation well.

claim: The projection into the first three principal components does not provide greater insight than the first two.
source: Furthermore, the projection into the first three principal components does not provide greater insight.
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of PCA for this data.

claim: Principal component analysis provides some information about the structure of the data, but does not permit easy visualization of its full structure in two or three dimensions.
source: Therefore, principal component analysis provides some information about the structure of the data, but does not permit easy visualization of its full structure in two or three dimensions.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of PCA for this data.

claim: UMAP minimizes the cross-entropy between topological representations of the local distance metric on some high-dimensional data manifold and on a low-dimensional embedding manifold.
source: UMAP minimizes the cross-entropy between topological representations of the local distance metric on some high-dimensional data manifold and on a low-dimensional embedding manifold.
evidence: This is a description of how UMAP works.

claim: UMAP is ideal for this application because it attempts to preserve the local and global topology of the high-dimensional data.
source: Among nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques, UMAP is ideal for this application because it attempts to preserve the local and global topology of the high-dimensional data, in contrast to algorithms like t-SNE, which is designed to emphasize local structure at the expense of global structure (Becht et al., 2019; McInnes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a justification for the choice of UMAP, supported by citations.

claim: t-SNE is designed to emphasize local structure at the expense of global structure.
source: Among nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques, UMAP is ideal for this application because it attempts to preserve the local and global topology of the high-dimensional data, in contrast to algorithms like t-SNE, which is designed to emphasize local structure at the expense of global structure (Becht et al., 2019; McInnes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a characterization of t-SNE, supported by citations.

claim: The data was represented by a bell-shaped manifold embedded in three-dimensional space.
source: Our data was represented by a bell-shaped manifold embedded in three-dimensional space (Figure 4).
evidence: This is the result of the UMAP embedding.

claim: The linear dimension along the axis of the bell is parameterized by the mean stepping frequency.
source: The linear dimension along the axis of the bell is parameterized by the mean stepping frequency (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), while the cyclic coordinate is defined by a single global phase (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in the UMAP embedding colored by frequency.

claim: The cyclic coordinate of the manifold is defined by a single global phase.
source: The linear dimension along the axis of the bell is parameterized by the mean stepping frequency (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), while the cyclic coordinate is defined by a single global phase (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in the UMAP embedding colored by limb position.

claim: Antiphase between contralateral limbs is preserved at all phases of the global oscillator.
source: Antiphase between contralateral limbs is preserved at all phases of the global oscillator (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is observed in the UMAP embedding colored by contralateral limb positions.

claim: Embedding individual trajectories illustrates a clockwise rotation during forward walking when viewed from the mouth of the bell.
source: Embedding individual trajectories illustrates a clockwise rotation during forward walking when viewed from the mouth of the bell (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is observed in the UMAP embedding of example trajectories.

claim: The number of feet in stance at the central timepoint of the sampled segments oscillates as a two-cycle as a function of the cyclic coordinate.
source: The number of feet in stance at the central timepoint of the sampled segments oscillates as a two-cycle as a function of the cyclic coordinate (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is observed in the UMAP embedding colored by number of feet in stance.

claim: The density of points within the manifold along its axial dimension is unimodal.
source: Consistent with the absence of multiple preferred configuration patterns, the density of points within this manifold along its axial dimension is unimodal (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in the distribution of points along the UMAP axial dimension.

claim: If one halves or doubles the segment length, the axial extent of the manifold is compressed or extended.
source: If one halves or doubles the segment length, the axial extent of the manifold is compressed or extended, intuitively corresponding to one's ability to extract frequency information from the time series, following the frequency-time uncertainty principle (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is observed in UMAP embeddings with different segment lengths.

claim: The manifold learning analysis reveals a structure that exactly corresponds to the intuitive representation of a system of coupled oscillators with a shared frequency that varies between segments.
source: Thus, this manifold learning analysis of our data reveals a structure that exactly corresponds to the intuitive representation of a system of coupled oscillators with a shared frequency that varies between segments.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the UMAP results.

claim: The simple model recapitulated several key observations in the data.
source: This simple construction recapitulated several key observations in our data.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's performance.

claim: The model can generate canonical tripod and wave gaits, as well as a continuum of intermediate coordination patterns.
source: First, it can generate canonical tripod and wave gaits, as well as a continuum of intermediate coordination patterns (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model outputs.

claim: Because the phase difference across the body is always one half-cycle, the model cannot produce the canonical tetrapod gait, but it can produce the tetrapod-like pattern with a characteristic offset in swings observed in experimental data.
source: Importantly, because the phase difference across the body is always one half-cycle, this model cannot produce the canonical tetrapod gait, but it can produce the tetrapod-like pattern with a characteristic offset in swings observed in our experimental data.
evidence: This is a property of the model that matches the experimental observations.

claim: With an appropriate choice of stance duration, the model generated the observed non-canonical limb pattern in which fore- and hind-limbs swing simultaneously while mid-limbs swing individually.
source: With an appropriate choice of stance duration, it also generated the observed non-canonical limb pattern in which fore- and hind-limbs swing simultaneously while mid-limbs swing individually.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model outputs.

claim: With the model, the number of feet in stance phase varied as a function of the forward walking speed, as observed in experimental data.
source: With this model, the number of feet in stance phase varied as a function of the forward walking speed, as observed in experimental data (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a comparison of model output to experimental data.

claim: The model reproduced the measured two-cycle in the number of feet down as a function of limb phase.
source: The model also reproduced the measured two-cycle in the number of feet down as a function of limb phase (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparison of model output to experimental data.

claim: The two-cycle occurs in the model because each ipsilateral posterior-to-anterior wave is effectively a single event, and they are always exactly out of phase.
source: This two-cycle occurs in the model because each ipsilateral posterior-to-anterior wave is effectively a single event, and they are always exactly out of phase.
evidence: This is an explanation of why the model produces the two-cycle.

claim: The mean contralateral relative phases are constant across forward walking speeds in the model, while the mean ipsilateral relative phases vary in a speed-dependent manner, consistent with experiments.
source: The mean contralateral relative phases are constant across forward walking speeds, while the mean ipsilateral relative phases vary in a speed-dependent manner, consistent with our experiments (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a comparison of model output to experimental data.

claim: The model recapitulates the decrease in variance in the relative phases with increasing forward speed observed in the data.
source: Finally, this model recapitulates the decrease in variance in the relative phases with increasing forward speed observed in our data (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a comparison of model output to experimental data.

claim: Embedding the model-generated data using UMAP produces a single manifold, consistent with experimental observations.
source: Consistent with experimental observations, embedding the model-generated data using UMAP produces a single manifold (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a comparison of model output to experimental data.

claim: This simple model with speed-independent limb coupling and a single control parameter qualitatively captures major characteristics of the symmetric variability in Drosophila spontaneous walking coordination.
source: Overall, this simple model with speed-independent limb coupling and a single control parameter qualitatively captures major characteristics of the symmetric variability in Drosophila spontaneous walking coordination.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's performance.

claim: The path length differential during turning could be achieved by modulating any combination of three parameters of limb kinematics: the frequency of stepping, the length of steps, and the direction of steps.
source: This path length differential could be achieved by modulating any combination of three parameters of limb kinematics: the frequency of stepping, the length of steps, and the direction of steps.
evidence: This is a logical enumeration of possible mechanisms for turning.

claim: On average, the swing durations of the inside mid- and hind-limbs decrease as a function of turning rate, while their stance durations increase.
source: On average, the swing durations of the inside mid- and hind-limbs decrease as a function of turning rate, while their stance durations increase (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: The swing and stance durations of the outside limbs are oppositely modulated compared to inside limbs during turning.
source: The swing and stance durations of the remaining limbs are oppositely modulated (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: At the highest yaw rates, the net modulation of stepping frequency is about 25%.
source: At the highest yaw rates, the net modulation of stepping frequency is about 25%.
evidence: This is a quantification from the experimental data.

claim: The step length of the inside forelimb is not significantly modulated during turning.
source: The step length of the inside forelimb is not significantly modulated during turning (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: The step lengths of the outside limbs increase with yaw rate while step lengths of the inside midlimb and hindlimb decrease with increasing turning rate.
source: The step lengths of the outside limbs increase with yaw rate while step lengths of the inside midlimb and hindlimb decrease with increasing turning rate.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: The observed limb-specific modulations of step frequency and step length are consistent with reports in other hexapods.
source: Overall, the observed limb-specific modulations of step frequency and step length are consistent with reports in other hexapods (Franklin et al., 1981; Frantsevich and Mokrushov, 1980; Graham, 1972; Gruhn et al., 2016; Jindrich and Full, 1999; Strauß and Heisenberg, 1990; Zollikofer, 1994; Zolotov et al., 1975).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature.

claim: The direction of steps in the inside and outside forelimbs is shifted such that their movements are directed outwards relative to the curvature of the path.
source: The direction of steps in the inside and outside forelimbs is shifted such that their movements are directed outwards relative to the curvature of its path.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: The fly achieves the required difference in forelimb path length by directing forelimb motions away from, rather than along, its path.
source: This suggests that the fly achieves the required difference in forelimb path length by directing forelimb motions away from, rather than along, its path.
evidence: This is an inference from the step direction data.

claim: The forelimb step direction modulation is consistent with measurements in cockroaches and in tethered stick insects.
source: This is consistent with measurements in cockroaches (Jindrich and Full, 1999; Mu and Ritzmann, 2005) and in tethered stick insects (Gruhn et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature.

claim: Unlike forward walking speed changes, which are dominated by global modulations of a single parameter, turns are achieved through asymmetric and limb-specific modulations of multiple parameters of limb movement.
source: Thus, unlike forward walking speed changes, which are dominated by global modulations of a single parameter, turns are achieved through asymmetric and limb-specific modulations of multiple parameters of limb movement.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings on turning versus speed modulation.

claim: Turns are preferentially aligned to a particular phase for each leg, which corresponds to a preferred phase of the walking oscillator.
source: Turns were preferentially aligned to a particular phase for each leg, which corresponds to a preferred phase of the walking oscillator (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This is observed in the analysis of limb phases at yaw extrema.

claim: There exists a statistically significant difference between the distributions of phases for all timepoints and for yaw extrema (p<10−5 for all limbs).
source: In particular, there exists a statistically significant difference between the distributions of phases for all timepoints and for yaw extrema (p<10−5 for all limbs, see Materials and methods, Table 4).
evidence: This is the result of statistical testing.

claim: Turns consist of precisely-timed modulations of the underlying walking coordination pattern, which couple the asymmetric variability to the symmetric coordination patterns.
source: Thus, turns consist of precisely-timed modulations of the underlying walking coordination pattern, which couple the asymmetric variability to the symmetric coordination patterns.
evidence: This is an inference from the phase-locked timing of turns.

claim: Short-timescale activation of moonwalker neurons caused a transient reduction in forward walking speed that lasted ~100 ms.
source: Short-timescale activation of moonwalker neurons caused a transient reduction in forward walking speed that lasted ~100 ms (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is observed in the optogenetic experiments.

claim: The reduction in forward walking speed from moonwalker activation is consistent with the suppression of forward walking elicited by activating a subset of the moonwalker neurons.
source: This slowing is consistent with the suppression of forward walking elicited by activating a subset of the moonwalker neurons (Bidaye et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature.

claim: The reduction in forward walking speed from moonwalker activation was accompanied by a transient increase in stance duration.
source: This reduction in forward walking speed was accompanied by a transient increase in stance duration, the control parameter for speed regulation in our coordination model (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is observed in the optogenetic experiments.

claim: In individual trials, all limbs increased their stance duration over hundreds of milliseconds in response to the brief neural activation.
source: In individual trials, all limbs increased their stance duration over hundreds of milliseconds in response to the brief neural activation (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is observed in individual trial examples.

claim: When visualized using UMAP, moonwalker activation corresponded to a deflection along the stepping frequency dimension of the manifold, consistent with a modulation of stance duration.
source: When visualized using UMAP, moonwalker activation corresponded to a deflection along the stepping frequency dimension of the manifold, consistent with a modulation of stance duration (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is observed in the UMAP embedding of optogenetic trials.

claim: Symmetrically activating a small subset of command neurons shifts the fly's limb coordination along the same manifold as spontaneous symmetric variation.
source: Thus, symmetrically activating a small subset of command neurons shifts the fly's limb coordination along the same manifold as spontaneous symmetric variation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Previous studies in tethered and freely-walking flies have shown that a variety of visual stimuli evoke slowing.
source: Previous studies in tethered and freely-walking flies have shown that a variety of visual stimuli evoke slowing (Creamer et al., 2018; Katsov and Clandinin, 2008; Silies et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In response to visual stimulus, flies slowed transiently, consistent with previous studies.
source: In response to this visual stimulus, flies slowed transiently, consistent with previous studies (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is observed in the visual stimulus experiments and consistent with previous work.

claim: As with the moonwalker manipulation, visual stimulation produced a transient increase in stance durations.
source: As with the moonwalker manipulation, visual stimulation produced a transient increase in stance durations (Figure 8F–G).
evidence: This is observed in the visual stimulus experiments.

claim: The visual stimulus-based perturbations induced shifts along the frequency dimension of the UMAP manifold, corresponding to the change in stance duration.
source: The visual stimulus-based perturbations also induced shifts along the frequency dimension of the UMAP manifold, corresponding to the change in stance duration (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is observed in the UMAP embedding of visual stimulus trials.

claim: Slowing evoked by visual stimuli generated transient changes along the same manifold as the spontaneous symmetric modulations that control walking speed.
source: Therefore, slowing evoked by visual stimuli generated transient changes along the same manifold as the spontaneous symmetric modulations that control walking speed.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the visual stimulus experiments.

claim: A central component of computational models of hexapod locomotion is the nature of inter-limb coupling, which in turn determines the predicted limb coordination patterns.
source: A central component of these models is the nature of inter-limb coupling, which in turn determines the predicted limb coordination patterns.
evidence: This is a statement about the structure of computational models.

claim: The simple model suggests that one might expect to find mutual inhibitory coupling between contralateral neuropil of the ventral nerve cord (VNC) and posterior to anterior inhibitory coupling between ipsilateral neuropil.
source: Our simple model suggests that one might expect to find mutual inhibitory coupling between contralateral neuropil of the ventral nerve cord (VNC) and posterior to anterior inhibitory coupling between ipsilateral neuropil.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model about neural circuit organization.

claim: Neither contralateral nor ipsilateral couplings need vary with walking speed.
source: Importantly, neither contralateral nor ipsilateral couplings need vary with walking speed.
evidence: This is a property of the model.

claim: If a single continuum can describe fly walking, then models of the circuit controlling walking may be made substantially simpler, since they need not account for multiple distinct coordination patterns.
source: If a single continuum can describe fly walking, then models of the circuit controlling walking may be made substantially simpler, since they need not account for multiple distinct coordination patterns.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings for circuit models.

claim: A simpler control circuit need only be able to vary stance duration while maintaining ipsilateral and contralateral coupling.
source: Instead, a simpler control circuit need only be able to vary stance duration while maintaining ipsilateral and contralateral coupling.
evidence: This is an inference about the requirements for a control circuit.

claim: Walking Drosophila may use a qualitatively different locomotor control circuit than previously studied animals in which distinct gaits have been observed.
source: This suggests the intriguing possibility that walking Drosophila may use a qualitatively different locomotor control circuit than previously studied animals in which distinct gaits have been observed (Alexander, 1989; Alexander and Jayes, 1980; Alexander and Jayes, 1983; Brett and Sutherland, 1965; Rayner et al., 1986; Srinivasan and Ruina, 2006).
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: There were aspects of the experimental data that were not captured by the simple model.
source: However, there were aspects of our experimental data that were not captured by our simple model.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the model's limitations.

claim: The magnitude of ipsilateral relative phase shifts is larger in the model than in the data, with greater deviations at slow forward walking speeds.
source: Though the ipsilateral relative phases exhibited qualitatively similar speed-dependent shifts, the magnitude of these shifts is larger in our model than in our data, with greater deviations at slow forward walking speeds.
evidence: This is a comparison of model output to experimental data.

claim: The experimental data included turning, which the model does not consider.
source: First, our experimental data included turning, which our model does not consider.
evidence: This is an explanation for differences between model and data.

claim: The relative timing of ipsilateral swings was less variable in the model than in the experimental data.
source: Second, the relative timing of ipsilateral swings was less variable in our model than in our experimental data.
evidence: This is a comparison of model output to experimental data.

claim: Each swing event in the model was of constant duration while experimentally-measured swings were more variable in duration overall and shorter on average at slow forward walking speeds.
source: Third, each swing event in the model was of constant duration while our experimentally-measured swings were more variable in duration overall and shorter on average at slow forward walking speeds.
evidence: This is a comparison of model output to experimental data.

claim: These differences do not diminish the utility of the simple model, since its purpose is to illustrate the sufficiency of a single set of couplings to describe the symmetric variability in spontaneous limb coordination.
source: These differences do not diminish the utility of this simple model, since its purpose is to illustrate the sufficiency of a single set of couplings to describe the symmetric variability in spontaneous limb coordination.
evidence: This is a statement about the purpose and utility of the model.

claim: Prior studies have suggested that the inter-limb coordination patterns used by insects reflect an optimization against physical constraints.
source: Prior studies have suggested that the inter-limb coordination patterns used by insects reflect an optimization against physical constraints (Nishii, 2000; Szczecinski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Theoretical work has suggested that continua of coordination patterns minimize the energetic cost of transport when ground reaction forces are balanced across limbs.
source: Theoretical work has suggested that continua of coordination patterns, like those identified here in Drosophila, minimize the energetic cost of transport when ground reaction forces are balanced across limbs (Nishii, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Distinct gaits are optimal when non-uniform ground reaction forces are necessary to balance the body.
source: In contrast, distinct gaits are optimal when non-uniform ground reaction forces are necessary to balance the body (Nishii, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: The magnitude and robustness of mechanical stability during walking may also influence the presence or absence of distinct gaits.
source: The magnitude and robustness of mechanical stability during walking may also influence the presence or absence of distinct gaits (Szczecinski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The simple control of the observed continuum of coordination patterns might make it preferable in animals with small circuits for controlling limbs.
source: In addition to these mechanical considerations, we suggest that the simple control of the observed continuum of coordination patterns might make it preferable in animals with small circuits for controlling limbs.
evidence: This is speculation about the advantages of a continuum control strategy.

claim: The asymmetric variability in limb kinematics associated with turning represents a minor modification of the coordination patterns used during forward walking, with ~25% modulations of limb movement parameters at the highest yaw rates.
source: The asymmetric variability in limb kinematics associated with turning represents a minor modification of the coordination patterns used during forward walking, with ~25% modulations of limb movement parameters at the highest yaw rates.
evidence: This is a summary of the turning results.

claim: Detailed neuromechanical and phase-reduced models in cockroaches have shown that ~20% modulations in forelimb placement parameters can generate 90° degree turns within three strides.
source: Detailed neuromechanical and phase-reduced models in cockroaches (Kukillaya and Holmes, 2009; Kukillaya et al., 2009; Proctor and Holmes, 2018; Proctor et al., 2010) and simplified bipedal models (Proctor and Holmes, 2008) have shown that ~20% modulations in forelimb placement parameters can generate 90° degree turns within three strides.
evidence: This is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: These theoretical findings are consistent with experimental results in cockroaches, which show that limb kinematics and dynamics during turning represent a minor modification of the symmetric coordination pattern.
source: These theoretical findings are consistent with experimental results in cockroaches, which show that limb kinematics and dynamics during turning represent a minor modification of the symmetric coordination pattern (Jindrich and Full, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: The small magnitude of turning modulations suggests a conceptual parallel between turning during walking and during flight.
source: The small magnitude of these modulations suggests a conceptual parallel between turning during walking and during flight.
evidence: This is speculation about a parallel between walking and flight control.

claim: In flying Drosophila, detailed kinematic and dynamical measurements and modeling have shown that yaw is regulated through small modulations of wing rotation angle while gross wingbeat movements remain mostly unaffected.
source: In flying Drosophila, detailed kinematic and dynamical measurements and modeling have shown that yaw is regulated through small modulations of wing rotation angle while gross wingbeat movements remain mostly unaffected (Dickinson and Muijres, 2016; Fry et al., 2003; Lindsay et al., 2017; Muijres et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of flight control.

claim: Mechanically, turning could be achieved through asymmetric modulations of limb movement that do not affect the coordination between ipsilateral limbs.
source: Mechanically, turning could be achieved through asymmetric modulations of limb movement that do not affect the coordination between ipsilateral limbs (Proctor and Holmes, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to modeling work.

claim: The command signals regulating turning could be unilateral but not segment-specific if turning were achieved through asymmetric modulations that do not affect ipsilateral coordination.
source: In this case, the command signals regulating turning could be unilateral but not segment-specific.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be required if turning worked in a particular way.

claim: Swing duration, stance duration, step length, and step direction are all modulated on an individual-limb basis during turning.
source: However, swing duration, stance duration, step length, and step direction are all modulated on an individual-limb basis during turning.
evidence: This is a summary of the turning results.

claim: The motor output of individual limbs in freely-walking flies is regulated during turning at the hemi-segmental level by control signals.
source: This suggests that the motor output of individual limbs in freely-walking flies is regulated during turning at the hemi-segmental level by control signals, a conclusion which is consistent with electrophysiological measurements and pharmacological manipulations in dissected stick insects (Gruhn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by citation to work in stick insects.

claim: Forward speed changes are associated primarily with modulations in stance duration that are comparable across all limbs.
source: In contrast to the limb-specific modulation of many kinematic degrees of freedom during turning, forward speed changes are associated primarily with modulations in stance duration that are comparable across all limbs (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a summary of the speed modulation results.

claim: The fact that limb movements are modulated along different dimensions for yaw and speed control suggests differentiation between the circuit bases of symmetric and asymmetric variability beyond the simple requirement of asymmetric limb movement in turning.
source: The fact that limb movements are modulated along different dimensions for yaw and speed control suggests differentiation between the circuit bases of symmetric and asymmetric variability beyond the simple requirement of asymmetric limb movement in turning.
evidence: This is an inference about circuit organization based on the different control strategies.

claim: As turns are precisely timed relative to the walking coordination pattern, the control of these symmetric and asymmetric modulations must be neurally or mechanically coupled.
source: However, as turns are precisely timed relative to the walking coordination pattern (Figure 7), the control of these symmetric and asymmetric modulations must be neurally or mechanically coupled.
evidence: This is an inference from the phase-locked timing of turns.

claim: The observed complexity in symmetric interlimb coordination can be reproduced with fixed, unidirectional posterior-to-anterior coupling between limbs.
source: Our detailed characterization of walking suggests that, surprisingly, the observed complexity in symmetric interlimb coordination can be reproduced with fixed, unidirectional posterior-to-anterior coupling between limbs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling work.

claim: The model implies that the most posterior of the limb neuropils could have a differentiated role in walking speed regulation, as swing events originate in these posterior segments.
source: This model implies that the most posterior of the limb neuropils could have a differentiated role in walking speed regulation, as swing events originate in these posterior segments.
evidence: This is an inference from the model structure.

claim: Anatomical evidence supports a differentiated role for the posterior neuropil.
source: Anatomical evidence supports this differentiated role.
evidence: This is a statement that anatomical data is consistent with the model prediction.

claim: The moonwalker ascending neurons receive dendritic input almost exclusively from the metathoracic neuromere, with axons projecting to more anterior neuropils in the thorax and to the subesophageal ganglion.
source: In particular, the moonwalker ascending neurons receive dendritic input almost exclusively from the metathoracic neuromere, with axons projecting to more anterior neuropils in the thorax and to the subesophageal ganglion (Bidaye et al., 2014).
evidence: This is anatomical information from previous work.

claim: Moonwalker neurons' activation causes the fly to slow its walking.
source: Their activation causes the fly to slow its walking (Bidaye et al., 2014), and they appear most active when all six limbs are in stance phase (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Moonwalker neurons appear most active when all six limbs are in stance phase.
source: Their activation causes the fly to slow its walking (Bidaye et al., 2014), and they appear most active when all six limbs are in stance phase (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Kinematic measurements suggest that the forelimbs, and thus the anterior neuropil, play a distinct role in spontaneous turning.
source: In contrast, our kinematic measurements suggest that the forelimbs, and thus the anterior neuropil, play a distinct role in spontaneous turning, a result consistent with dynamical measurements in cockroaches (Jindrich and Full, 1999).
evidence: This is an inference from the turning data, supported by citation to work in cockroaches.

claim: Symmetry arguments suggest that walking speed and turning must be regulated through different coordinated patterns of neural activity.
source: Symmetry arguments suggest that walking speed and turning must be regulated through different coordinated patterns of neural activity.
evidence: This is a logical argument based on symmetry considerations.

claim: The difference in the roles of anterior and posterior neuropils in the two locomotor behaviors supports a hypothesis that these behaviors employ distinct circuitry.
source: The difference in the roles of anterior and posterior neuropils in the two locomotor behaviors supports a hypothesis that these behaviors employ distinct circuitry.
evidence: This is an inference from the different roles of neuropils in speed and turning control.

claim: A variety of studies have demonstrated that tonic activation of descending neurons (DNs) suffices to generate complex, structured motor patterns in the fruit fly.
source: Despite the phasic relationships between limbs during locomotion and grooming, a variety of studies have demonstrated that tonic activation of descending neurons (DNs) suffices to generate complex, structured motor patterns in the fruit fly (Bidaye et al., 2014; Cande et al., 2018; Seeds et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous electrophysiological recordings in orthopteran insects showed that neurons projecting from the insect brain to the thoracic ganglia are tonically active in all regions except for those emanating from the subesophageal ganglion.
source: Interestingly, previous electrophysiological recordings in orthopteran insects showed that neurons projecting from the insect brain to the thoracic ganglia are tonically active in all regions except for those emanating from the subesophageal ganglion (Heinrich, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The organization of descending neurons suggests that the control of motor behaviors in insects physically segregates action selection and the low-level implementation of motor behaviors into the brain and VNC respectively.
source: This organization suggests that the control of motor behaviors in insects physically segregates action selection and the low-level implementation of motor behaviors into the brain and VNC respectively.
evidence: This is an inference from the organization of descending neurons.

claim: The manifold structure of limb coordination is compatible with tonic descending inputs that modulate limb movements, while local circuits in the VNC coordinate limbs.
source: The manifold structure of limb coordination is compatible with tonic descending inputs that modulate limb movements, while local circuits in the VNC coordinate limbs.
evidence: This is an inference about how the manifold structure relates to circuit organization.

claim: Explorations of VNC circuits are increasingly made possible by automated behavioral tracking, preparations to visualize neural activity in the VNC, genetic tools to target neurons in the VNC, and tools to manipulate neural activity.
source: These experiments have shown that variability in walking coordination patterns exists on a continuous manifold. In Drosophila, explorations of VNC circuits are increasingly made possible by automated behavioral tracking (Branson et al., 2009; Mathis et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2019; Williamson et al., 2018), by preparations to visualize neural activity in the VNC (Chen et al., 2018; Tuthill and Wilson, 2016), and by genetic tools to target neurons in the VNC (Cande et al., 2018; Mamiya et al., 2018; Namiki et al., 2018) and to manipulate neural activity (Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent methodological advances.

claim: The manifold structure of limb coordination in Drosophila provides a framework for dissecting the circuits that regulate walking.
source: The manifold structure of limb coordination in Drosophila provides a framework for dissecting the circuits that regulate walking.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings for future research.
